---
title: "Revision and integration"
---

The questions combine material from all units of each half of the course.
Answer each question before opening its answer.

## Animal half {#animal-half}

### 1.1

Put the steps in order for an oxygen molecule moving from the atmosphere to a
mitochondrion in a mammalian skeletal-muscle fibre:

a. O₂ binds to haemoglobin in a red blood cell
b. O₂ dissociates from haemoglobin in a systemic capillary
c. inspired air moves through the conducting airways to the alveoli
d. blood flows through the pulmonary veins, left atrium, left ventricle and
   systemic arteries
e. O₂ diffuses across the alveolar wall and capillary endothelium into the plasma
f. O₂ diffuses through interstitial fluid into the muscle fibre and is reduced
   to water by the mitochondrial electron transport chain

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

c → e → a → d → b → f. Steps c and d are bulk flow (ventilation and
circulation); steps e and f are diffusion down a partial-pressure gradient.
:::

### 1.2

Two animals, each of mass 0.5 g, consume 18 and 30 µmol O₂ in 6 minutes.

a. Calculate the whole-animal rate of oxygen consumption for each animal.
b. Calculate the mass-specific rate for each animal.
c. The two animals were measured at different temperatures and had different
   feeding histories. True or false: the data show that temperature caused the
   difference in rate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 18/6 = 3 µmol O₂ min⁻¹ and 30/6 = 5 µmol O₂ min⁻¹.
b. 3/0.5 = 6 µmol O₂ min⁻¹ g⁻¹ and 5/0.5 = 10 µmol O₂ min⁻¹ g⁻¹.
c. False. Temperature and feeding history differ together (they are
   confounded), so the effect of either cannot be separated.
:::

### 1.3

The metabolic rate of an ectotherm is 2 units at 10 °C and 8 units at 30 °C.
Calculate $Q_{10}$ for this interval.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$Q_{10} = (R_2/R_1)^{10/(T_2-T_1)} = (8/2)^{10/20} = 4^{0.5} = 2$.
:::

### 1.4

Over one day an animal ingests 200 kJ. Its faeces contain 50 kJ, its excreted
nitrogenous waste contains 10 kJ and its metabolic expenditure is 120 kJ.
Calculate:

a. the absorbed energy
b. the retained energy (growth and storage)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 200 − 50 = 150 kJ day⁻¹.
b. 200 − 50 − 10 − 120 = 20 kJ day⁻¹.
:::

### 1.5

A person at rest has a cardiac output of 5 L min⁻¹, an arterial O₂ content of
200 mL O₂ L⁻¹ and a mixed-venous O₂ content of 150 mL O₂ L⁻¹. During heavy
exercise, cardiac output is 20 L min⁻¹ and mixed-venous O₂ content falls to
100 mL O₂ L⁻¹, while arterial content is unchanged.

a. Calculate the whole-body O₂ consumption at rest and during exercise.
b. By what factor did O₂ consumption increase?
c. By what factors did cardiac output and the arterial–venous O₂ difference
   change?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Rest: 5 × (200 − 150) = 250 mL O₂ min⁻¹.
   Exercise: 20 × (200 − 100) = 2000 mL O₂ min⁻¹.
b. 2000/250 = 8 times.
c. Cardiac output increased 4 times; the arterial–venous difference doubled
   (50 → 100 mL O₂ L⁻¹). 4 × 2 = 8.
:::

### 1.6

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. A rightward shift of the haemoglobin–oxygen dissociation curve means a higher
   oxygen affinity.
b. Higher temperature, higher CO₂ and lower pH shift the curve to the right.
c. Blood with a normal O₂ partial pressure but a low haemoglobin concentration
   has a normal O₂ content.
d. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. A rightward shift means lower affinity: a higher partial pressure is
   needed for the same saturation, which favours unloading in the tissues.
b. True.
c. False. Most O₂ in blood is bound to haemoglobin, so less haemoglobin means
   lower O₂ content at the same partial pressure.
d. True. Veins carry blood towards the heart; the name does not depend on the
   oxygen content.
:::

### 1.7

Classify each event as ingestion, digestion, absorption, egestion or excretion.

a. Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses triglycerides in the small intestine.
b. Glucose crosses the intestinal epithelium into the blood.
c. Undigested plant fibre leaves the body in the faeces.
d. Urea leaves the body in the urine.
e. A cow takes grass into its mouth.

In a ruminant, does microbial fermentation take place before or after the small
intestine?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Digestion. b. Absorption. c. Egestion. d. Excretion. e. Ingestion.

Before: fermentation occurs in the rumen, so microbes and their products then
pass on to the small intestine.
:::

### 1.8

Complete the table for typical teleost fishes.

| | Freshwater teleost | Marine teleost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body fluids compared with the surrounding water (hyperosmotic or hypo-osmotic) | | |
| Passive water movement across gills and skin | | |
| Passive ion movement across gills and skin | | |
| Drinking | | |
| Urine | | |
| Active ion transport at the gills | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Freshwater teleost | Marine teleost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body fluids compared with the surrounding water | Hyperosmotic | Hypo-osmotic |
| Passive water movement across gills and skin | Gain | Loss |
| Passive ion movement across gills and skin | Loss | Gain |
| Drinking | Little or none | Drinks seawater |
| Urine | Large volume, dilute | Small volume, about isosmotic to plasma |
| Active ion transport at the gills | Uptake of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ | Secretion of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ |
:::

### 1.9

Assume complete dissociation and that the inside of a red blood cell is about
0.30 Osm L⁻¹.

a. Calculate the osmolarity of 0.15 mol L⁻¹ NaCl, 0.30 mol L⁻¹ sucrose and
   0.30 mol L⁻¹ urea.
b. Red blood cells are placed in each solution. The membrane is impermeable to
   Na⁺, Cl⁻ and sucrose but permeable to urea. State whether each solution is
   isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic to the cells.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. All three are 0.30 Osm L⁻¹ (NaCl gives two particles per formula unit).
b. NaCl: isotonic. Sucrose: isotonic. Urea: hypotonic. Urea enters the cells,
   water follows, and the cells swell and lyse. The solutions are isosmotic,
   but they do not have the same tonicity.
:::

### 1.10

For substance X: plasma concentration 2 mmol L⁻¹, glomerular filtration rate
0.12 L min⁻¹, tubular reabsorption 0.20 mmol min⁻¹, tubular secretion
0.01 mmol min⁻¹ and urine flow 0.002 L min⁻¹. Calculate:

a. the filtered load of X
b. the excretion rate of X
c. the concentration of X in the urine

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 2 mmol L⁻¹ × 0.12 L min⁻¹ = 0.24 mmol min⁻¹.
b. 0.24 − 0.20 + 0.01 = 0.05 mmol min⁻¹.
c. 0.05 mmol min⁻¹ / 0.002 L min⁻¹ = 25 mmol L⁻¹.
:::

### 1.11

Put these parts of a mammalian nephron in the order that filtrate passes
through them: distal tubule, Bowman's capsule, collecting duct, ascending limb
of the loop of Henle, proximal tubule, descending limb of the loop of Henle.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → descending limb → ascending limb →
distal tubule → collecting duct.
:::

### 1.12

Plasma osmolality rises after a mammal loses water. Match each item to its role
in the feedback loop: regulated variable, sensor, effector, signal.

a. antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)
b. collecting-duct epithelial cells
c. plasma osmolality
d. osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus

What does ADH change in the collecting duct, and what happens to urine volume
and concentration?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. signal; b. effector; c. regulated variable; d. sensor.

ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct by inserting
aquaporins into the apical membrane. More water is reabsorbed into the
hyperosmotic medulla, so urine volume falls and urine concentration rises.
This is negative feedback: the response lowers plasma osmolality.
:::

### 1.13

Complete the table of nitrogenous wastes.

| | Ammonia | Urea | Uric acid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Toxicity | | | |
| Water needed for excretion | | | |
| Energy cost of synthesis | | | |
| Example animal group | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Ammonia | Urea | Uric acid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Toxicity | High | Low | Very low |
| Water needed for excretion | Much | Moderate | Little |
| Energy cost of synthesis | None (direct product) | Moderate | Highest |

### 1.14

Put the steps in order, from a motor-neuron action potential to skeletal-muscle
contraction:

a. Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
b. acetylcholine binds to receptors on the muscle fibre
c. the action potential reaches the motor-neuron terminal
d. Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, and tropomyosin moves to expose binding sites on actin
e. voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters the nerve terminal
f. myosin cross-bridges cycle, using ATP
g. an action potential spreads along the muscle membrane and into the T-tubules
h. acetylcholine is released into the synaptic cleft

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

c → e → h → b → g → a → d → f.
:::

### 1.15

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. The inside of a resting neuron is negative relative to the outside.
b. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into it for each ATP
   hydrolysed.
c. A stronger stimulus produces larger action potentials in a sensory neuron.
d. Whole-muscle force can be increased by recruiting more motor units.
e. ATP is needed for myosin to detach from actin.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. True.
b. True.
c. False. Action potentials are all-or-none with a roughly fixed amplitude.
   A stronger stimulus increases their frequency (and may recruit more neurons).
d. True.
e. True. Without ATP, cross-bridges stay attached (as in rigor mortis).
:::

### 1.16

Name the gland or tissue that secretes or releases each hormone.

a. GnRH
b. LH and FSH
c. ADH (released into the blood)
d. insulin
e. oestrogen

Which type of feedback from oestrogen produces the LH surge that triggers
ovulation?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Hypothalamus. b. Anterior pituitary. c. Posterior pituitary (it is made by
hypothalamic neurons). d. β-cells of the pancreatic islets. e. Ovary (follicle cells).

Positive feedback: sustained high oestrogen increases GnRH/LH release.
:::

## Plant half {#plant-half}

### 2.1

A plant cell has Ψs = −1.2 MPa and Ψp = +0.5 MPa.

a. Calculate its water potential.
b. State the initial direction of net water movement when the cell is placed in
   pure water (Ψ = 0 MPa), and in a solution with Ψ = −0.9 MPa.
c. A root cell has Ψ = −0.4 MPa. In which direction does water initially move
   when the soil solution is −0.1 MPa, and when a saline soil solution is
   −0.6 MPa?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Ψ = Ψs + Ψp = −1.2 + 0.5 = −0.7 MPa.
b. Pure water: into the cell. −0.9 MPa solution: out of the cell. Water moves
   from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) potential.
c. −0.1 MPa soil: into the root cell. −0.6 MPa saline soil: out of the root cell.
:::

### 2.2

Arrange from highest to lowest water potential in a transpiring plant: leaf
mesophyll cell walls, atmosphere, soil water, root xylem.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Soil water → root xylem → leaf mesophyll cell walls → atmosphere. Water moves
passively down this gradient; the largest drop is from the leaf to the air.
:::

### 2.3

a. Put the steps in order for water moving from the soil to the atmosphere:

   1. evaporation from mesophyll cell walls into the leaf air spaces
   2. entry into a root hair
   3. crossing the endodermis
   4. diffusion of water vapour out through a stoma
   5. movement through the root cortex
   6. bulk flow up the xylem of the stem

b. What structure forces water and solutes to cross a plasma membrane at the
   endodermis, and what is it made of?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 2 → 5 → 3 → 6 → 1 → 4.
b. The Casparian strip, a band of suberin (and lignin) in the radial and
   transverse walls of endodermal cells. It blocks the apoplastic route.
:::

### 2.4

Complete the table.

| | Xylem | Phloem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conducting cells | | |
| Living at functional maturity? | | |
| Main substances transported | | |
| Direction of flow | | |
| Pressure in the conducting cells | | |
| Source of the driving force | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Xylem | Phloem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conducting cells | Tracheids and vessel elements | Sieve-tube elements (with companion cells) |
| Living at functional maturity? | No | Yes (without a nucleus) |
| Main substances transported | Water and mineral ions | Sucrose and other assimilates |
| Direction of flow | From roots to shoots | From sources to sinks (up or down) |
| Pressure in the conducting cells | Negative (tension) | Positive |
| Source of the driving force | Evaporation from leaves (cohesion–tension) | Loading of sugar at sources draws in water osmotically (pressure flow) |
:::

### 2.5

Match each description to one cell type: parenchyma, collenchyma,
sclerenchyma, guard cell, companion cell.

a. Living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls that support growing stems
b. Cells with thick lignified secondary walls, often dead at maturity
c. Thin-walled living cells used for photosynthesis or storage
d. Paired epidermal cells that border a pore
e. A nucleated cell connected to a sieve-tube element by many plasmodesmata

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Collenchyma. b. Sclerenchyma. c. Parenchyma. d. Guard cell. e. Companion cell.
:::

### 2.6

a. Put the steps of stomatal opening in order:

   1. water enters the guard cells by osmosis
   2. blue light activates the plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase of the guard cells
   3. guard-cell turgor rises and the pore opens
   4. K⁺ (with Cl⁻ and malate) accumulates in the guard cells
   5. the membrane hyperpolarises and K⁺ channels open

b. Which hormone causes stomatal closure during drought?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 2 → 5 → 4 → 1 → 3.
b. Abscisic acid (ABA). It causes K⁺ and anion efflux from the guard cells, so
   water leaves, turgor falls and the pore closes.
:::

### 2.7

Net CO₂ uptake of a leaf (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured at four light
intensities (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹):

| Light | 0 | 50 | 200 | 800 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Net CO₂ uptake | −2 | 0 | 6 | 9 |

a. What is the rate of respiration in darkness?
b. At which light intensity is the light compensation point?
c. Assume that respiration in the light equals respiration in the dark.
   Calculate gross photosynthesis at 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
d. True or false: at the light compensation point, photosynthesis and
   respiration have stopped.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 2 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ (CO₂ release).
b. About 50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, where net uptake is zero.
c. Gross = net + respiration = 6 + 2 = 8 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
d. False. Both continue; CO₂ uptake by photosynthesis equals CO₂ release by
   respiration.
:::

### 2.8

a. Complete the table.

| | Light-dependent reactions | Calvin–Benson cycle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location in the chloroplast | | |
| Inputs | | |
| Outputs | | |

b. Three CO₂ fixed in the Calvin–Benson cycle give one triose phosphate and
   use 9 ATP and 6 NADPH. How much CO₂, ATP and NADPH are needed for one
   glucose (two triose phosphates)?

c. What is the source of the O₂ released in photosynthesis?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

**a.**

| | Light-dependent reactions | Calvin–Benson cycle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location in the chloroplast | Thylakoid membranes | Stroma |
| Inputs | Light, H₂O, ADP + Pᵢ, NADP⁺ | CO₂, ATP, NADPH (and RuBP, regenerated) |
| Outputs | O₂, ATP, NADPH | Triose phosphate, ADP + Pᵢ, NADP⁺ |

b. 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
c. Water, split at photosystem II.
:::

### 2.9

Complete the table.

| | C3 | C4 | CAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enzyme that first fixes CO₂ | | | |
| First stable product | | | |
| How initial fixation is separated from the Calvin–Benson cycle | | | |
| When stomata are mainly open | | | |
| Photorespiration in hot, bright conditions | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | C3 | C4 | CAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enzyme that first fixes CO₂ | Rubisco | PEP carboxylase | PEP carboxylase |
| First stable product | 3-phosphoglycerate (3C) | Oxaloacetate (4C) | Oxaloacetate (4C), stored as malate |
| How initial fixation is separated from the Calvin–Benson cycle | Not separated | In space: mesophyll and bundle-sheath cells | In time: night and day |
| When stomata are mainly open | Day | Day | Night |
| Photorespiration in hot, bright conditions | High | Low | Low |
:::

### 2.10

Classify each organ as a source or a sink of sugar.

a. a mature, illuminated leaf
b. a developing fruit
c. a growing root tip
d. a potato tuber sprouting in spring
e. a young, expanding leaf

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Source. b. Sink. c. Sink. d. Source (its stored starch is mobilised for the
new shoots). e. Sink.
:::

### 2.11

Match each plant hormone to one response: auxin, gibberellin, abscisic acid,
ethylene, cytokinin, jasmonate, salicylic acid.

a. ripening of climacteric fruits such as tomato and banana
b. bending of a shoot towards light
c. stem elongation and breaking of seed dormancy
d. cell division in shoot meristems
e. stomatal closure and maintenance of seed dormancy
f. defence against chewing insects after wounding
g. defence against biotrophic pathogens

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Ethylene. b. Auxin. c. Gibberellin. d. Cytokinin. e. Abscisic acid.
f. Jasmonate. g. Salicylic acid.
:::

### 2.12

a. Name the photoreceptor family that detects (i) red and far-red light and
   (ii) blue light for phototropism.
b. Under a leaf canopy the ratio of red to far-red light falls. What growth
   response does this cause in a shade-avoiding seedling?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. (i) Phytochromes. (ii) Phototropins (cryptochromes also detect blue light).
b. Increased stem and petiole elongation (shade-avoidance response).
:::

### 2.13

a. Classify each case as dormancy or quiescence:
   (i) a dry seed stored in a packet;
   (ii) a viable seed in warm, moist soil that will not germinate until it has
   been exposed to cold.
b. Twelve of 20 seeds have germinated by day 5. Calculate the germination
   percentage.
c. True or false: the other eight seeds are dead.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. (i) Quiescence: external conditions (water) are unsuitable.
   (ii) Dormancy: a viable seed does not germinate under otherwise suitable
   conditions.
b. 12/20 × 100 = 60%.
c. False. They may be dormant, may germinate later or may be non-viable; the
   count alone cannot tell.
:::

### 2.14

a. Match each element to one role: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium,
   iron.

   1. central atom of chlorophyll
   2. part of amino acids and nucleotides
   3. main ion for osmotic adjustment in guard cells
   4. part of ATP and nucleic acids
   5. component of cytochromes and electron-transfer proteins

b. Nitrogen is mobile in the phloem; iron is not. In which leaves do deficiency
   symptoms of each first appear?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Magnesium: 1. Nitrogen: 2. Potassium: 3. Phosphorus: 4. Iron: 5.
b. Nitrogen: older leaves, because it is remobilised to new growth.
   Iron: young leaves, because it cannot be moved out of older leaves.
:::

### 2.15

Classify each example as an acute response, acclimation or evolutionary
adaptation.

a. Stomata close within minutes after the roots are exposed to drying soil.
b. Plants grown for several weeks in cool conditions increase the proportion of
   unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes.
c. A desert population has inherited CAM photosynthesis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Acute response. b. Acclimation. c. Evolutionary adaptation.
:::

### 2.16

Match each term to its definition: transformation, regeneration, promoter,
reporter gene, genome editing, *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*.

a. a DNA sequence that controls where and when a gene is transcribed
b. a bacterium that transfers a DNA segment (T-DNA) into plant cells
c. the introduction of foreign DNA into a cell
d. a targeted change in an existing DNA sequence of the organism
e. the growth of a whole plant from cultured cells or tissue
f. a gene whose product is easy to detect, such as GFP or GUS

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Promoter. b. *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*. c. Transformation.
d. Genome editing. e. Regeneration. f. Reporter gene.
:::

## Integrating both halves {#integration}

### 3.1

Classify each movement as diffusion, osmosis, bulk flow or primary active
transport.

a. blood flowing through the aorta
b. O₂ crossing the alveolar wall
c. sap rising in the xylem
d. sucrose solution moving along sieve tubes
e. H⁺ pumped out of a root cell by the plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase
f. Na⁺ moved out of a neuron by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
g. CO₂ moving from a leaf air space into a mesophyll cell
h. water entering a guard cell through aquaporins

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Bulk flow. b. Diffusion. c. Bulk flow. d. Bulk flow.
e. Primary active transport. f. Primary active transport. g. Diffusion.
h. Osmosis.
:::

### 3.2

Complete the table comparing water movement into the root xylem of a plant and
out of the collecting duct of a mammalian kidney.

| | Plant root | Mammalian collecting duct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is water actively pumped? | | |
| Membrane proteins that increase water permeability | | |
| Origin of the gradient that drives water movement | | |
| Structure that blocks the route between cells | | |
| Hormone that reduces water loss from the organism | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Plant root | Mammalian collecting duct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is water actively pumped? | No | No |
| Membrane proteins that increase water permeability | Aquaporins | Aquaporins |
| Origin of the gradient that drives water movement | Lower water potential in the xylem, mainly from transpiration (and solutes loaded into the xylem) | High osmolality of the medullary interstitium, built by ion transport in the loop of Henle and by urea |
| Structure that blocks the route between cells | Casparian strip | Tight junctions |
| Hormone that reduces water loss from the organism | Abscisic acid (stomatal closure) | ADH (more water reabsorbed) |

In both cases active ion transport creates the gradient, and water follows
passively.
:::

### 3.3

Complete the table comparing three gas-exchange organs.

| | Fish gill | Mammalian lung | Leaf |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | | | |
| Exchange surface | | | |
| Pattern of flow of the medium | | | |
| Gas mainly taken up in daylight | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Fish gill | Mammalian lung | Leaf |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | Water | Air | Air |
| Exchange surface | Gill lamellae | Alveoli | Walls of mesophyll cells facing the air spaces |
| Pattern of flow of the medium | One-way, countercurrent to blood | Tidal (in and out by the same airways) | No ventilation; diffusion through stomata |
| Gas mainly taken up in daylight | O₂ | O₂ | CO₂ |
:::

### 3.4

State whether each process produces O₂, consumes O₂ or neither.

a. photosynthetic electron transport at photosystem II
b. mitochondrial respiration in a leaf cell in the light
c. mitochondrial respiration in a muscle fibre
d. photorespiration
e. lactate fermentation in muscle
f. ethanol fermentation in a waterlogged root

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Produces. b. Consumes. c. Consumes. d. Consumes (Rubisco oxygenation).
e. Neither. f. Neither.
:::

### 3.5

A red blood cell and a plant cell are both placed in pure water. The red blood
cell bursts; the plant cell does not. Name the structure responsible for the
difference, and the pressure that builds up in the plant cell.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The cell wall. Turgor (pressure potential, Ψp) rises until the water potential
of the cell equals that of the surrounding water, so net water entry stops.
:::
